latin-world.name: Latin-script languages of Asia and Africa

Russian.tell: Russian has ы, э and ъ, and no і. The letters ї, є, ґ (Ukrainian) and ў (Belarusian) never appear.
sentences: Я хотел бы заказать чашку чая.
I would like to order a cup of tea.
Завтра мы поедем на дачу.
Tomorrow we're going to the summer house.
Где находится ближайшая станция метро?
Where is the nearest metro station?

Ukrainian.tell: і, ї, є and ґ are Ukrainian letters. Ukrainian has no ы, э or ъ, which are very common in Russian.
sentences: Я хотів би замовити чашку чаю.
I would like to order a cup of tea.
Завтра ми поїдемо до бабусі в село.
Tomorrow we'll go to grandma's in the village.
Де знаходиться найближча станція метро?
Where is the nearest metro station?

Belarusian.tell: ў (u with a breve) is found only in Belarusian. It uses і like Ukrainian, but also ы and э like Russian.
sentences: Я хацеў бы замовіць кубак гарбаты.
I would like to order a cup of tea.
Заўтра мы паедзем да бабулі ў вёску.
Tomorrow we'll go to grandma's in the village.
Дзе знаходзіцца бліжэйшая станцыя метро?
Where is the nearest metro station?

Bulgarian.tell: Bulgarian uses ъ as an ordinary vowel (съм, във) and never has ы or э. Nouns carry 'the' as an ending: -та, -то, -ът.
sentences: Бих искал чаша кафе, моля.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Утре отиваме на море с приятелите.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside with friends.
Къде е най-близката спирка на автобуса?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Serbian.tell: Serbian has its own letters ђ and ћ, and also uses ј, љ, њ and џ. It has no я, ю, щ or ы.
sentences: Желео бих шољу кафе, молим.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Сутра идемо на море са пријатељима.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside with friends.
Где је најближа аутобуска станица?
Where is the nearest bus station?

Macedonian.tell: ѓ and ќ are found only in Macedonian (ѕ is rare elsewhere too). Like Serbian it uses ј, љ, њ, but not ђ or ћ.
sentences: Би сакал една кафе, ве молам.
I would like a coffee, please.
Утре одиме на езеро со пријателите.
Tomorrow we're going to the lake with friends.
Каде е најблиската автобуска станица?
Where is the nearest bus station?

Kazakh.tell: Kazakh adds ә, ғ, қ, ң, ө, ұ, ү, һ and і to the Russian alphabet. ә, қ and ұ are the giveaways.
sentences: Маған бір кесе шай беріңізші.
Please give me a cup of tea.
Ертең біз тауға барамыз.
Tomorrow we're going to the mountains.
Қазақстан өте үлкен ел.
Kazakhstan is a very big country.

Mongolian.tell: Mongolian uses ө and ү a lot, often doubled (өө, үү, аа), but has none of Kazakh's ә, ғ, қ.
sentences: Би нэг аяга цай уумаар байна.
I would like to drink a cup of tea.
Маргааш бид хөдөө явна.
Tomorrow we're going to the countryside.
Монгол улс их өргөн уудам.
Mongolia is very vast.

Spanish.tell: ñ, and questions that start with ¿ or ¡, are uniquely Spanish. There's lots of 'que', 'el' and 'los', and words ending in -ción.
sentences: Me gustaría pedir una taza de café con leche, por favor.
I would like to order a cup of coffee with milk, please.
Mañana vamos a visitar a mis abuelos en el pueblo.
Tomorrow we're going to visit my grandparents in the village.
¿Dónde está la biblioteca más cercana?
Where is the nearest library?

Portuguese.tell: ã and õ (with a tilde) and endings like -ção, -ções are Portuguese. Look for 'não', 'você' and 'muito'.
sentences: Eu gostaria de um café sem açúcar, por favor.
I would like a coffee without sugar, please.
Amanhã vamos à praia com os nossos amigos.
Tomorrow we're going to the beach with our friends.
Não consigo encontrar as minhas chaves em lado nenhum.
I can't find my keys anywhere.

French.tell: French has many accents (é, è, ê, à, ç), apostrophes (l', d', j', qu') and silent endings (-ent, -ez). Look for 'je', 'est', 'les' and 'vous'.
sentences: Je voudrais réserver une table pour deux personnes ce soir.
I would like to book a table for two people this evening.
Il fait très beau aujourd'hui, allons nous promener.
The weather is lovely today, let's go for a walk.
Où se trouve la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
Where is the train station, please?

Italian.tell: Almost every Italian word ends in a vowel, and there are lots of double consonants (-tt-, -ll-, -zz-). Look for 'che', 'gli', 'sono' and 'il'.
sentences: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
I would like a glass of water, please.
Domani andiamo al mare con i nostri amici.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside with our friends.
Non ho mai visto un tramonto così bello.
I've never seen such a beautiful sunset.

Romanian.tell: ă, â, î, ș and ț are Romanian. The 'the' goes on the end of words: 'prietenii' means 'the friends'.
sentences: Aș dori o cafea cu lapte, vă rog.
I would like a coffee with milk, please.
Mâine mergem la munte cu prietenii.
Tomorrow we're going to the mountains with friends.
Unde este cea mai apropiată stație de autobuz?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Catalan.tell: Catalan has l·l (with a middle dot), à, è, ò, and words ending in -ny or -ix. Look for 'amb', 'és', 'els', 'molt' and 'més'.
sentences: Voldria un cafè amb llet, si us plau.
I would like a coffee with milk, please.
Demà anirem a la platja amb els amics.
Tomorrow we'll go to the beach with our friends.
La ciutat és molt més bonica a la nit.
The city is much more beautiful at night.

English.tell: English has no accents at all, and uses lots of 'the', 'th', 'w' and words like 'is', 'and' and 'you'.
sentences: The weather is lovely today, so let's go for a walk in the park.
I forgot my umbrella at the office again.
Could you tell me where the nearest train station is?

German.tell: ß, plus ä, ö and ü, are German. Every noun starts with a capital letter. Look for 'ich', 'nicht', 'und' and 'sch'.
sentences: Ich habe gestern einen sehr interessanten Film gesehen.
Yesterday I saw a very interesting film.
Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen, den Bahnhof zu finden?
Could you please help me find the train station?
Wir fahren im Sommer mit dem Fahrrad an die Ostsee.
In summer we're cycling to the Baltic Sea.

Dutch.tell: The 'ij' combination and double vowels (aa, ee, oo, uu) are Dutch. Look for 'het', 'een', 'niet' and 'zijn'.
sentences: Ik heb gisteren een heel mooi boek gelezen.
Yesterday I read a really nice book.
Waar is het dichtstbijzijnde station?
Where is the nearest station?
We gaan dit weekend fietsen langs de grachten.
This weekend we're cycling along the canals.

Afrikaans.tell: Afrikaans looks like simplified Dutch. It puts 'nie' twice in negative sentences, uses 'is' and 'het' for everyone, and has ê and ë. Look for 'ek' (I) and 'jy' (you).
sentences: Ek wil graag 'n koppie koffie hê, asseblief.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Ons gaan môre strand toe met ons vriende.
Tomorrow we're going to the beach with our friends.
Ek het nie my sleutels gekry nie.
I didn't find my keys.

Swedish.tell: Swedish uses ä and ö (like German), where Norwegian and Danish use æ and ø. Look for 'och', 'jag' and 'inte'.
sentences: Jag skulle vilja ha en kopp kaffe, tack.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Vi ska åka till landet i sommar.
We're going to the countryside this summer.
Hur mycket kostar den här tröjan?
How much does this sweater cost?

Norwegian.tell: Norwegian has æ, ø and å like Danish, but it's spelled closer to how it sounds: 'meg', 'deg' and 'hva', where Danish has 'mig', 'dig' and 'hvad'. Look for 'ikke' and 'jeg'.
sentences: Jeg liker å gå på tur i fjellet om helgene.
I like hiking in the mountains at weekends.
Hvor ligger nærmeste bensinstasjon?
Where is the nearest petrol station?
Vi spiste middag hos bestemor i går.
We had dinner at grandma's yesterday.

Danish.tell: Danish has æ, ø and å like Norwegian, but with 'soft' spellings like 'mig', 'dig', 'hvad' and 'af', and endings like -de and -ge.
sentences: Jeg vil gerne have en kop kaffe, tak.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Vi cykler til stranden i morgen tidlig.
We're cycling to the beach early tomorrow.
Hvad hedder du, og hvor kommer du fra?
What's your name, and where are you from?

Icelandic.tell: þ (thorn) and ð (eth) are the giveaways. Only Icelandic still uses þ; Faroese has ð but not þ.
sentences: Ég elska að horfa á norðurljósin á veturna.
I love watching the northern lights in winter.
Hvar er næsta sundlaug?
Where is the nearest swimming pool?
Veðrið er mjög gott í dag.
The weather is very good today.

Polish.tell: ł, ą, ę, ś, ć, ź and ż are Polish, along with lots of 'sz', 'cz' and 'rz'. It has no č or š.
sentences: Chciałbym zamówić kawę z mlekiem, proszę.
I would like to order a coffee with milk, please.
Jutro jedziemy w góry z przyjaciółmi.
Tomorrow we're going to the mountains with friends.
Gdzie jest najbliższy przystanek autobusowy?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Czech.tell: ř, ě and ů (u with a ring) are found only in Czech.
sentences: Zítra pojedeme na výlet do hor.
Tomorrow we're going on a trip to the mountains.
Kde je nejbližší zastávka tramvaje?
Where is the nearest tram stop?
Dám si jedno pivo, prosím.
I'll have a beer, please.

Slovak.tell: Slovak has ä, ô, ľ, ĺ and ŕ, but none of Czech's ř, ě or ů.
sentences: Zajtra pôjdeme na výlet do hôr.
Tomorrow we're going on a trip to the mountains.
Kde je najbližšia zastávka električky?
Where is the nearest tram stop?
Dám si jedno pivo, prosím. Ďakujem!
I'll have a beer, please. Thank you!

Slovene.tell: Slovene uses only three special letters (č, š, ž), with no ć or đ like Croatian. Look for 'je', 'sem' and 'bom'.
sentences: Jutri gremo na izlet v hribe.
Tomorrow we're going on a trip to the hills.
Kje je najbližja avtobusna postaja?
Where is the nearest bus station?
Rad bi eno kavo z mlekom, prosim.
I'd like a coffee with milk, please.

Croatian.tell: Croatian has both č and ć, plus đ (d with a stroke). Look for 'je', 'sam', 'ću' and 'što'.
sentences: Sutra idemo na more s prijateljima.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside with friends.
Gdje je najbliža autobusna stanica?
Where is the nearest bus station?
Htio bih šalicu kave, molim.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.

Finnish.tell: Finnish has lots of doubled vowels and consonants (aa, ää, kk, tt), ä and ö, and very long words. It has no b, f or š in native words.
sentences: Minä rakastan saunomista talvella.
I love going to the sauna in winter.
Missä on lähin rautatieasema?
Where is the nearest railway station?
Tänään on todella kaunis päivä.
Today is a really beautiful day.

Estonian.tell: õ is the Estonian giveaway. It looks like Finnish, with doubled letters and ä, ö and ü, but Finnish has no õ or ü.
sentences: Ma tahaksin tassi kohvi, palun.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Homme läheme sõpradega randa.
Tomorrow we're going to the beach with friends.
Kus on lähim bussipeatus?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Hungarian.tell: ő and ű (with a double accent) are found only in Hungarian. Look for 'sz', 'gy', 'cs' and 'zs'.
sentences: Szeretnék egy csésze kávét kérni.
I would like to ask for a cup of coffee.
Holnap elmegyünk a Balatonra.
Tomorrow we're going to Lake Balaton.
Hol van a legközelebbi metróállomás?
Where is the nearest metro station?

Lithuanian.tell: Lithuanian has ą, ę, į and ų (with a little hook underneath) plus ė and ū. Words often end in -as, -is or -us.
sentences: Norėčiau puodelio kavos, prašau.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Rytoj važiuojame prie jūros su draugais.
Tomorrow we're going to the seaside with friends.
Kur yra artimiausia autobusų stotelė?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Latvian.tell: Latvian marks long vowels with a line (ā, ē, ī, ū) and has ķ, ļ, ņ and ģ (with a comma underneath).
sentences: Es vēlētos tasi kafijas, lūdzu.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
Rīt mēs brauksim uz jūru ar draugiem.
Tomorrow we'll drive to the sea with friends.
Kur ir tuvākā autobusa pietura?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Arabic.tell: Arabic has lots of ال ('al-', meaning 'the') at the start of words and ة at word ends, but none of the extra letters پ, چ, ژ or گ used in Persian and Urdu.
sentences: أود أن أطلب فنجان قهوة من فضلك.
I would like to order a cup of coffee, please.
سنذهب إلى البحر غداً مع أصدقائنا.
We'll go to the sea tomorrow with our friends.
أين أقرب محطة قطار؟
Where is the nearest train station?

Persian.tell: Persian adds پ, چ, ژ and گ. Look for 'است' (is), 'می' before verbs, and few ال or ة.
sentences: می‌خواهم یک فنجان چای سفارش بدهم.
I want to order a cup of tea.
فردا با دوستانم به کوه می‌رویم.
Tomorrow I'm going to the mountains with my friends.
نزدیک‌ترین ایستگاه مترو کجاست؟
Where is the nearest metro station?

Urdu.tell: Urdu has ٹ, ڈ and ڑ (with a small ط on top) and ے at word ends. Look for 'ہے' (is) at the end of sentences.
sentences: مجھے ایک کپ چائے چاہیے۔
I want a cup of tea.
کل ہم اپنے دوستوں کے ساتھ بازار جائیں گے۔
Tomorrow we'll go to the market with our friends.
سب سے قریبی ریلوے اسٹیشن کہاں ہے؟
Where is the nearest railway station?

Pashto.tell: Pashto has its own letters ښ, ږ, ځ, څ and ړ, and ې and ۍ at word ends.
sentences: زه یوه پیاله چای غواړم.
I want a cup of tea.
سبا موږ بازار ته ځو.
Tomorrow we're going to the market.
ته څنګه یې؟
How are you?

Hindi.tell: Hindi uses Devanagari, with a line along the top of the letters. Sentences often end in 'है' or 'हैं' and '।'.
sentences: मुझे एक कप चाय चाहिए।
I want a cup of tea.
कल हम अपने दोस्तों के साथ बाज़ार जाएँगे।
Tomorrow we'll go to the market with our friends.
सबसे नज़दीकी रेलवे स्टेशन कहाँ है?
Where is the nearest railway station?

Nepali.tell: Nepali uses the same Devanagari script as Hindi, but sentences end in 'छ', 'छु' or 'हो' instead of 'है'.
sentences: मलाई एक कप चिया चाहियो।
I want a cup of tea.
भोलि हामी साथीहरूसँग बजार जान्छौं।
Tomorrow we're going to the market with friends.
नेपाल सुन्दर देश हो।
Nepal is a beautiful country.

Bengali.tell: Bengali also has a top line, but with triangle-shaped letters like ব, ক and ত, and 'আ' at the start of words.
sentences: আমি এক কাপ চা চাই।
I want a cup of tea.
আগামীকাল আমরা বন্ধুদের সাথে বাজারে যাব।
Tomorrow we'll go to the market with friends.
সবচেয়ে কাছের রেলস্টেশন কোথায়?
Where is the nearest railway station?

Punjabi.tell: Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi, which has a top line too. Look for ੳ and ੲ, and 'ਹੈ' at the end.
sentences: ਮੈਨੂੰ ਇੱਕ ਕੱਪ ਚਾਹ ਚਾਹੀਦੀ ਹੈ।
I need a cup of tea.
ਕੱਲ੍ਹ ਅਸੀਂ ਦੋਸਤਾਂ ਨਾਲ ਬਾਜ਼ਾਰ ਜਾਵਾਂਗੇ।
Tomorrow we'll go to the market with friends.
ਤੁਹਾਡਾ ਨਾਮ ਕੀ ਹੈ?
What is your name?

Tamil.tell: Tamil letters are round and loopy, with no line on top. Look for ழ and many 'ம்', 'ன்' endings with a dot on top.
sentences: எனக்கு ஒரு கப் டீ வேண்டும்.
I want a cup of tea.
நாளை நாங்கள் கடற்கரைக்கு போகிறோம்.
Tomorrow we're going to the beach.
உங்கள் பெயர் என்ன?
What is your name?

Thai.tell: Thai letters have little loops at the start of each stroke, and there are no spaces between words. Look for ๆ, and 'ครับ' or 'ค่ะ' at the end of sentences.
sentences: ขอกาแฟหนึ่งแก้วครับ
One coffee, please.
พรุ่งนี้เราจะไปทะเลกับเพื่อน
Tomorrow we're going to the sea with friends.
สถานีรถไฟที่ใกล้ที่สุดอยู่ที่ไหน
Where is the nearest train station?

Lao.tell: Lao looks like a rounder, simpler Thai, with fewer loops and fewer letters. Look for ຂ, ບ and ໃ, and 'ບໍ່' (not).
sentences: ສະບາຍດີ, ເຈົ້າສະບາຍດີບໍ່?
Hello, how are you?
ຂ້ອຍຢາກກິນເຂົ້າໜຽວ
I want to eat sticky rice.
ຂອບໃຈຫຼາຍໆ
Thank you very much.

Khmer.tell: Khmer is very ornate, with small letters stacked underneath others (subscripts). It looks 'taller' and busier than Thai or Lao.
sentences: សួស្តី តើអ្នកសុខសប្បាយទេ?
Hello, how are you?
ខ្ញុំចង់ញ៉ាំបាយ
I want to eat rice.
អរគុណច្រើន
Thank you very much.

Burmese.tell: Burmese letters are almost all built from circles and half-circles, like ဝ, ရ and မ.
sentences: မင်္ဂလာပါ
Hello.
ကျွန်တော် ထမင်းစားချင်တယ်
I want to eat rice.
ကျေးဇူးတင်ပါတယ်
Thank you.

Chinese.tell: Chinese uses only characters (汉字), none of the curly Japanese kana (の, は, を) or Korean circles and lines.
sentences: 我想要一杯咖啡，谢谢。
I'd like a cup of coffee, thanks.
明天我们要去公园散步。
Tomorrow we're going for a walk in the park.
最近的地铁站在哪里？
Where is the nearest metro station?

Japanese.tell: Japanese mixes Chinese characters with simple curly kana like の, は, を, ます and katakana like コーヒー.
sentences: コーヒーを一杯お願いします。
One coffee, please.
明日は友達と海に行きます。
Tomorrow I'm going to the sea with friends.
一番近い駅はどこですか？
Where is the nearest station?

Korean.tell: Korean Hangul builds syllable blocks from circles (ㅇ), lines and angles, like 커피, and words are separated by spaces.
sentences: 커피 한 잔 주세요.
A cup of coffee, please.
내일 친구들과 바다에 갈 거예요.
Tomorrow I'll go to the sea with friends.
가장 가까운 지하철역이 어디예요?
Where is the nearest subway station?

Greek.tell: The Greek alphabet has α, β, γ, δ, λ, π, σ and ς (a final s), with accents on the stressed vowel (ά, ή, ό).
sentences: Θα ήθελα ένα ποτήρι νερό, παρακαλώ.
I would like a glass of water, please.
Αύριο θα πάμε στη θάλασσα.
Tomorrow we'll go to the sea.
Πού είναι ο πλησιέστερος σταθμός του μετρό;
Where is the nearest metro station?

Georgian.tell: Georgian's rounded, bubbly letters (ა, ბ, გ, დ) have no capitals and no top line.
sentences: გამარჯობა, როგორ ხარ?
Hello, how are you?
მე მიყვარს საქართველო.
I love Georgia.
დიდი მადლობა.
Thank you very much.

Armenian.tell: Armenian letters look a bit like Latin letters with hooks and tails (ե, ի, ս). Look for the common pair 'ու'.
sentences: Բարև, ինչպե՞ս ես։
Hello, how are you?
Ես սիրում եմ Հայաստանը։
I love Armenia.
Շնորհակալություն։
Thank you.

Hebrew.tell: Hebrew is written right to left in square letters with no joining between them (unlike Arabic). Look for ש, ה and ם.
sentences: הייתי רוצה כוס קפה, בבקשה.
I would like a cup of coffee, please.
מחר אנחנו נוסעים לים עם חברים.
Tomorrow we're going to the sea with friends.
איפה התחנה הקרובה ביותר?
Where is the nearest station?

Amharic.tell: Amharic (Ge'ez script) uses syllable symbols with little legs and loops, like ሰ, ላ, ም, separated by ፡ or spaces.
sentences: ሰላም፣ እንዴት ነህ?
Hello, how are you?
ቡና እወዳለሁ።
I love coffee.
አመሰግናለሁ።
Thank you.

Turkish.tell: ı (i without a dot) and ğ are Turkish, along with ş, ç, ö and ü. Turkish has no ə.
sentences: Bir fincan çay alabilir miyim, lütfen?
Could I have a cup of tea, please?
Yarın arkadaşlarımla denize gideceğiz.
Tomorrow we'll go to the seaside with my friends.
En yakın otobüs durağı nerede?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Azerbaijani.tell: ə (upside-down e) is the Azerbaijani giveaway. It also uses q and x more than Turkish does.
sentences: Mən bir fincan çay istəyirəm.
I want a cup of tea.
Sabah dostlarımla dənizə gedəcəyik.
Tomorrow we'll go to the sea with my friends.
Ən yaxın avtobus dayanacağı haradadır?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Uzbek.tell: Uzbek writes oʻ and gʻ with an apostrophe-like mark, and uses 'sh' and 'ch' instead of ş and ç. It has no ı or ə.
sentences: Men bir piyola choy ichmoqchiman.
I want to drink a cup of tea.
Ertaga doʻstlarim bilan bozorga boramiz.
Tomorrow we're going to the market with my friends.
Eng yaqin avtobus bekati qayerda?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Vietnamese.tell: Vietnamese stacks accents on vowels (ế, ộ, ữ) and has ư, ơ, ă and đ. Words are short, usually one syllable each.
sentences: Tôi muốn gọi một ly cà phê sữa đá.
I'd like to order an iced coffee with milk.
Ngày mai chúng tôi sẽ đi biển với bạn bè.
Tomorrow we'll go to the beach with friends.
Ga tàu gần nhất ở đâu?
Where is the nearest train station?

Indonesian.tell: Indonesian has plain letters with no accents. Look for 'yang', 'dan', 'tidak' and 'saya', and Indonesian words like 'bisa' and 'mobil' where Malay says 'boleh' and 'kereta'.
sentences: Saya ingin memesan secangkir kopi.
I want to order a cup of coffee.
Besok kami akan pergi ke pantai bersama teman-teman.
Tomorrow we'll go to the beach with friends.
Apakah kamu bisa naik mobil ke sana?
Can you get there by car?

Malay.tell: Malay is almost the same as Indonesian. Malay words include 'boleh' (can), 'kereta' (car), 'awak' (you) and 'percuma' (free).
sentences: Saya hendak memesan secawan kopi.
I'd like to order a cup of coffee.
Boleh awak pergi ke sana dengan kereta?
Can you go there by car?
Esok kami akan pergi ke pantai bersama kawan-kawan.
Tomorrow we'll go to the beach with friends.

Tagalog.tell: Look for 'ng', 'mga', 'ang', 'sa' and 'ako', and repeated syllables like 'pupunta'.
sentences: Gusto ko ng isang tasang kape.
I'd like a cup of coffee.
Pupunta kami sa dagat bukas kasama ang mga kaibigan.
We're going to the sea tomorrow with friends.
Saan ang pinakamalapit na istasyon ng tren?
Where is the nearest train station?

Swahili.tell: Swahili words start with prefixes like ni-, wa-, ku-, ki- and m-, and end in vowels. Look for 'ch', 'ng' and 'na'.
sentences: Ningependa kikombe cha chai, tafadhali.
I would like a cup of tea, please.
Kesho tutaenda ufukweni na marafiki zetu.
Tomorrow we'll go to the beach with our friends.
Kituo cha basi kilicho karibu kiko wapi?
Where is the nearest bus stop?

Irish.tell: Irish has accents on vowels (á, é, í, ó, ú) and combinations like 'bh', 'mh', 'dh' and 'ch'. Look for 'tá' (is).
sentences: Conas atá tú?
How are you?
Tá áthas orm bualadh leat.
I'm glad to meet you.
Go raibh míle maith agat.
Thank you very much (literally: a thousand goods to you).

Welsh.tell: Welsh uses w and y as vowels, and has lots of 'dd', 'll' and 'ch'. Look for 'yn', 'y' and 'mae'.
sentences: Bore da! Sut wyt ti?
Good morning! How are you?
Rydw i'n hoffi coffi.
I like coffee.
Diolch yn fawr iawn.
Thank you very much.

Basque.tell: Basque isn't related to any other language. It uses lots of k, z, x, tx and tz, and words ending in -ak, -ko or -en. Look for 'eta' (and).
sentences: Kaixo, zer moduz?
Hello, how are you?
Kafe bat nahi dut, mesedez.
I'd like a coffee, please.
Eskerrik asko etortzeagatik.
Thanks for coming.

Maltese.tell: Maltese is related to Arabic but written in Latin letters: ħ, għ, ċ, ż and ġ are the giveaways.
sentences: Nixtieq kafè, jekk jogħġbok.
I'd like a coffee, please.
Grazzi ħafna!
Thank you very much!
Għada se mmorru l-baħar.
Tomorrow we'll go to the sea.

Albanian.tell: ë appears everywhere in Albanian, plus ç and combinations like 'xh', 'gj', 'dh' and 'sh'.
sentences: Unë dua një kafe, ju lutem.
I want a coffee, please.
Nesër do të shkojmë në det me shokët.
Tomorrow we'll go to the sea with friends.
Faleminderit shumë!
Thank you very much!
